t: Minimum Cost to Equalize Arrays Using Swaps
o: Free swaps arbitrarily permute elements within each array; only swapping nums1[i] with nums2[i] at the same index costs 1. So the question is: choose an orientation (keep or flip) for each column so that the resulting nums1 multiset equals the nums2 multiset, minimizing flips. First, feasibility: each value must appear an even number of times across both arrays combined, since each array must end up with half of them (Examples 1-3 illustrate 0, 1, and impossible). For each value v with p copies in nums1 and q in nums2, the target multiset needs h = (p+q)/2 copies; copies beyond p must come from flipping columns whose nums2 value is v, costing 1 each — giving a greedy lower bound of sum of max(0, h - p).
k: Feasible iff every value's combined count across both arrays is even.
Cost = sum over values v of max(0, (count(v) combined)/2 - count of v in nums1): each missing copy for the target multiset requires one cross swap.

a.i: The final common multiset must contain exactly half of each value's total occurrences. Columns holding that value in nums1 cover it for free; any shortfall must be supplied by flipping a column that holds the value in nums2, one cost apiece. Summing shortfalls over all values gives the minimum number of cross swaps.
s: Count occurrences of each value in nums1 (map ca) and nums2 (map cb).
For each value v in either map: if (ca[v] + cb[v]) is odd, return -1.
Add max(0, (ca[v] + cb[v]) / 2 - ca[v]) to the cost.
a.sp: O(n) for the two count maps.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask brute force over flip choices
a.i: For tiny n, try every subset of columns to flip; after applying flips, the arrays can be equalized for free iff their multisets match. This validates the greedy on small cases and is a good sanity harness.
s: For each mask in [0, 2^n): simulate flipping columns where the mask bit is set.
Track the minimum popcount among successful masks; return it or -1.
a.t: O(2^n · n log n) — exponential; only for very small n.

w: Present the counting greedy as the main O(n) solution and use the brute force only to justify it on small inputs. Pitfall: forgetting values that appear only in nums2 (their entire half must come from flips), and the odd-total impossibility check. Edge cases: arrays already equal as multisets (cost 0), disjoint value sets with even counts. Follow-up: what if cross swaps cost different amounts per index (becomes a min-cost matching/flow problem)?
